articles.summary: Bradley Whitford is ready to return to the White House. Hill said the cast wouldn’t hesitate if Sorkin decides to write a new season. “I always say that’s a question for Aaron Sorkin,” he said when asked about a revival. “If he writes it, then I will come. I think if he writes it, then we all will be there.”

articles.title: Gaza documentary NAZA beats Avengers Endgame: Encore to top Italian box office
articles.summary: Award-winning, Guardian-produced film focused on Israel’s mass killing of civilians extends run after sold-out screenings. NAZA, the award-winning documentary about Israel’s systemic mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza, has opened at No 1 at the Italian box office, beating rival titles…
body: The 80-minute film was booked for a three-day run in Italy, but after sold-out auditoriums and positive audience reaction, its release window will be extended. On its opening day on Monday, the documentary took a total of €451,872, with a per site average of €1,153.

By the end of Tuesday, this rose to about €1.1m. Avengers Endgame: Encore – a rerelease of the 2019 blockbuster featuring a new introduction and post-credits scene – made €356,000 over the same period.

Appetite in Italy was particularly primed for the film, which was directed by Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, and won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice film festival earlier this month. Its premiere a few days before was met with a 25-minute ovation – a festival record.

articles.title: Golden Globes Predictions: Let the Genre Games Begin for ‘Obsession,’ ‘Michael,’ ‘Wildwood’ and More
articles.summary: Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars, Emmys, Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis.
body: Golden Globes Predictions Commentary (Updated: Sept. 30, 2026): The Golden Globes submission deadline is coming up on Oct. 30, the night before Halloween. Fitting, since for the next 30 days, studios get to decide what costume their movies should wear for the early phase of awards season.

The Globes split their top film prize into two genres, drama and comedy/musical and the line between them has always been drawn by strategy as much as tone. Remember, this is the same awards show that “The Martian” once won best comedy.
For the third year in a row, the comedy/musical side looks more competitive than its drama counterpart. We’re used to seeing it the other way around, and several major players still haven’t declared.

On the drama side, Christopher Nolan’s summer blockbuster “The Odyssey” and “La Bola Negra,” the acclaimed epic from Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi (better known as Los Javis), lead the early pack. The Netflix title picked up the People’s Choice Award at the Toronto International Film Festival this month, four months after the duo won best director at Cannes. That bodes well for its run.

articles.title: Nicolas Cage Says the Marvel Cinematic Universe ‘Is Becoming a Well-Funded and Glorified WWE’ With 50-Plus Year Olds in ‘Ridiculous Outfits’
articles.summary: Nicolas Cage’s critique of the Marvel Cinematic Universe during a recent conversation at Fan Expo Dallas (via The Playlist) is quickly gaining traction on social media, with many people either agreeing with the Oscar-winning actor or questioning him considering his own ties to superhero projects.
body: Cage’s “Spider-Noir” series was based on the Marvel Comics character Spider-Man Noir and was adapted for television by Oren Uziel. The series took place during the Great Depression and starred Cage as Ben Reilly, “a seasoned, down-on-his-luck private investigator in 1930s New York, who is forced to grapple with his past life following a deeply personal tragedy, as the city’s one and only superhero.”

Speaking to Variety before the show’s premiere, Cage said he was attracted to “Spider-Noir” not because of its superhero roots but because the show was being designed in black and white as a classic film noir (and thus with shades of German expressionism thrown in).

“I wanted to try to create an essence of some of my favorite old world actors because I wanted to embody that style — Bogart, Cagney, Edward G. Robinson — and designed my performance to fit within the black-and-white format,” Cage said, adding that taking on a television show made him nervous at first.

articles.title: Veteran broadcaster Dame Esther Rantzen dies aged 86
articles.summary: Rantzen, who fronted the BBC's That's Life for two decades, went on to found Childline, and in recent years had been a campaigner for assisted dying.
body: Dame Esther Rantzen, who presented BBC show That's Life! for 21 years and launched the charity Childline, has died at the age of 86.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the veteran broadcaster and campaigner had "changed countless lives".
Dame Esther hosted and produced That's Life! during its run from 1973 to 1994. It regularly attracted 20 million viewers for its mixture of serious consumer investigations and light-hearted items.

She launched Childline, a British counselling service for children and young people, in 1986, and in 2013 she launched Silver Line to help elderly people suffering from isolation and loneliness. Later in life, she became a prominent campaigner for the legalisation of assisted dying.

articles.title: Post your questions for Michael Winterbottom
articles.summary: With us to mark the 24th anniversary of 24 Hour Party People, the director’s work includes everything from Cracker to A Cock and Bull Story, Wonderland to Welcome to Sarajevo. And, of course, The Trip.
body: Of course, the 90s couldn’t be any more in vogue at the minute – but the 90s couldn’t have happened without the 80s. And that’s where 24 Hour Party People comes in, Michael Winterbottom’s riotous 2002 film that charts Manchester’s music scene from the Sex Pistols’ legendary 1976 Lesser Free Trade Hall gig through Factory Records, Joy Division, New Order and into the Madchester era of Happy Mondays and the Haçienda. It’s the story of Manchester music before Oasis swaggered in and took over the world, and it stars Paddy Considine, Shirley Henderson, Andy Serkis and John Simm – plus Steve Coogan as the late broadcaster and Factory Records boss Tony Wilson.

He has also regularly reunited with Coogan, most famously for 2010’s The Trip and its sequels, in which Coogan and Brydon travelled, ate and attempted increasingly competitive celebrity impressions – including a Michael Caine-off that became almost as famous as the films themselves. The trio are now making a fifth instalment, The Trip to the Northern Lights, which sees Coogan and Brydon eating, bickering and impersonating their way through Scandinavia and the Nordic countries.

articles.title: Bayeux tour to include audio account of tapestry
articles.summary: The British Museum will offer an audio-described Bayeux Tapestry tour for people with impaired vision.
body: The British Museum will provide an audio-described tour of the Bayeux Tapestry after a man with visual impairment pointed out the lack of access for blind and partially-sighted people.
Dr Yusuf Ali Osman, from Croydon, said the museum breached the Equality Act by not offering such tours of the exhibition.
On Wednesday, the central London museum said an in-person audio-described tour would be held during the exhibition's run.
It said it was also exploring adding an audio-described tour to the exhibition's app.

articles.title: Cotton Queen review – mystery, matriarchs and magic in pioneering Sudanese debut
articles.summary: Suzannah Mirghani’s first feature contains a powerful performance by Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as a village’s elder woman and tackles the long shadow of British imperialism and women’s rights.
body: ‘I decide my past,” says a village matriarch in this intriguingly political and poetic drama from Suzannah Mirghani, making her feature debut – and with it becoming the first Sudanese woman to direct a feature. (She was forced to cancel the original shoot in Sudan when war broke out in 2023, moving production to Egypt.) It’s a film with things to say about the long shadow of the British empire, neocolonialism, women’s rights and female genital mutilation. But it mostly says it all without undermining its sense of mystery and shivers of magic realism.

We’re in present day Sudan, where village elder Al-Sit (Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud) is an iron-willed woman not to be messed with. Everyone knows the story of how as a young girl she ran the British out of town; small children in the village gleefully tell the story of how she slaughtered every single last one of them. Can it possibly be true? The trauma of her past is at the centre of the film, and Mahmoud’s witchy performance, fierce and powerful, is utterly compelling.

articles.title: How That's Life! gave Esther Rantzen a career-defining moment
articles.summary: Sir Nicholas Winton's story became national news when he appeared on That's Life! in February 1988.
body: Dame Esther Rantzen's commitment to charitable causes is something she will forever be remembered for.

Along with founding Childline, a helpline for children, and The Silver Line, which supports older people struggling with loneliness, she also created a broadcasting legacy during her time on That's Life!
She presented the hugely popular BBC One show from 1973 to 1994, helping transform it from a consumer rights programme to an issues-based series, drawing in huge audiences.
One of her most memorable career moments came during one particular episode in 1988 - the footage of which has gone viral several times over in recent years.

articles.title: Dame Esther Rantzen: That's Life! presenter, Childline founder and campaigner for assisted dying
articles.summary: The star presented That's Life! for two decades and set up two national helplines, including Childline.
body: Dame Esther Rantzen, who has died at the age of 86, was best known for presenting the BBC TV programme That's Life!
Over two decades, what started as a consumer programme with quirky asides became renowned for its high-profile campaigns, notably against child abuse.
It resulted in Dame Esther setting up Childline, a national telephone helpline for children suffering abuse or neglect.
She later became a renowned campaigner for older people and, in the last years of her life, for the legalisation of medically-assisted death.
